content.title: About
content.content: Millet is a group of small-seeded grasses cultivated in warm regions around the world. It has a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a light, fluffy texture when cooked. Millet is consumed as whole grain, flour, flakes, or puffed cereal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Millet is one of the oldest cultivated crops, with archaeological evidence dating back over 7,000 years.
It is highly drought‑tolerant and can grow on poor soils.
In many cultures millet is called the “golden grain” because of its bright yellow color.
Millet is naturally gluten‑free, making it suitable for gluten‑free diets.
In Africa and Asia millet is traditionally used for porridge, flatbreads, and fermented drinks.

items.title: Rich in magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in millet supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Iron helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds and vitamin E protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Millet raises blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber improves digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to millet.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting millet helps mitigate this.

items.title: Possible pesticide residues
items.content: As with other grains, choose certified organic or tested products to minimize exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Millet can be boiled as a porridge, added to salads, used in pilafs, baked into casseroles, or ground into flour for breads and pancakes. Rinsing and soaking the grains for 4–6 hours before cooking shortens the cooking time.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store millet in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
